chapter_title: Concerning why if a [Nail] is cut the Person shall

fills.notes: The syntax needs a finite verb: “these limbs also are of it,” matching the earth/body correspondence (earth : trees :: body : limbs).
The line is classifying “varieties … of tree,” then immediately continues with “There are others…,” so a simple taxonomic term is demanded.

In correspondential physiology, what “arises and grows again and stands firm” has a root (an interior connection); what “has not …” is what cannot regenerate after cutting. The contrast that follows (“others… cut shall not grow”) points to root/life-principle as the missing term.
Required by the repeated regeneration motif: some cut and regrow; others cut and do not.
The comparison is to another class already described (“like those which shall be cut and grow…”).
Completes the cycle: cut → grow → stand; maintains the parallelism with the first class of trees.
Introduces an additional subset: “and some … they too…,” preparing the next clause about those that occur and are cut.
“occur …” in this context is best constrained by a locality/source term (trees ‘occurring’ naturally vs cultivated). Correspondentially it marks spontaneous growth from the earth’s own state.
Sets up the double negation that follows (“neither grow nor shall they …”), maintaining the classification by regenerative capacity.
The natural sign of a tree’s inner life is fruit; in correspondence, fruit = effect/issue. Those that neither grow nor “bear fruit” fit the ‘dead’ class.
The phrase “it shall please him on …” needs an indeterminate object of choice/occasion: “on whatever (he chooses).”
Links the subject back to the tree/body analogue: “and it grows … in impurity … from him.”
Correspondentially, “impurity” produces disjunction; what grows “in impurity” is something that divides/estranges from its source (“from him”).

The surrounding sentence turns to “This flesh that is corrupt…,” so the missing portion at the page break should name the condition of corrupt flesh: admixture with death/decay as the opposite-sense life-principle.
The close reads: “in the living flesh and they … are somewhat sick.” The lacuna must supply a predicate of distress preceding “somewhat sick,” i.e., an intermediate state of suffering/affliction.

assessment: Most gaps can be constrained by the chapter’s fixed correspondence (body↔earth; limbs↔trees) and the repeated taxonomy of trees by regenerative power (cut/regrow vs cut/not regrow), which in the oldest layer maps to inner connection (root/life-principle) and outward effects (fruit). A few clauses near the end (impurity/page break) remain only tentatively recoverable because the immediate manuscript context is missing and multiple substrate-appropriate terms could fit.
